---
title: "Glossary — plain-language definitions"
---


Every term, symbol, and piece of project shorthand used in the notebook, in plain words. If a
notebook file uses something you don't recognize, it's defined here. Organized by topic, not
alphabetically, so related ideas sit together.

---

## The physics being measured

- **Charge trap (or "trap").** A defect in the silicon crystal that can grab a passing electron,
  hold it for a while, then let it go. That "let it go later" is the whole problem: an electron
  released long after the event that created it looks like a fresh single-electron signal.

- **Emission time, τ (tau), sometimes τ_e.** The average time a trap holds an electron before
  releasing it. Short τ = releases almost immediately; long τ = holds for hours, days, or longer.
  τ depends on temperature — warmer silicon releases faster.

- **τ135 (tau at 135 K).** The emission time τ *extrapolated to 135 K*, the operating temperature of
  the SENSEI experiment at SNOLAB. This is the axis that matters for the science, because a trap's
  danger is set by how long it holds charge at the operating temperature. Most traps are measured at
  *other* temperatures and τ135 is computed from a fitted model — so a "long-τ135" trap was usually
  never actually watched at 135 K (see "Arrhenius / SRH extrapolation").

- **Energy E and cross-section σ (sigma).** The two numbers that define a trap. **E** (in eV) is how
  deep the trap is — deeper traps hold charge longer. **σ** (an area, in cm²) is how big a target the
  trap presents to a passing electron — bigger σ = more likely to catch one. Together with
  temperature they predict τ at any temperature.

- **SRH (Shockley–Read–Hall).** The standard textbook model for how defects capture and emit charge
  carriers. It gives the formula `τ = exp(E/kT) / (σ · v_th · N_v)` linking a trap's τ to its E, σ,
  and the temperature T. "The SRH law" and "the Arrhenius fit" refer to fitting this to a trap's
  measured τ-vs-temperature points to extract E and σ.

- **Arrhenius extrapolation.** Because τ changes with temperature in a known (SRH) way, you can fit
  the trend and extend it to a temperature you never measured — how τ135 is obtained for traps that
  were only detectable when hot.

- **v_th, N_v, detailed balance (the pieces inside the SRH formula).** `v_th` = the typical thermal
  speed of a carrier; `N_v` = a temperature-dependent count of available quantum states ("effective
  density of states"). "Detailed balance" is the equilibrium principle that fixes the ratio of capture
  to emission; it's how the SRH formula is derived. You rarely need these directly — they're bundled
  constants.

- **Two-state / Markov kinetics.** The math for a trap that is either "empty" or "occupied" and hops
  between the two at capture and emission rates. "Exact two-state transition probability" just means
  the correct formula for the chance of ending a time-step occupied, allowing for multiple hops within
  the step — as opposed to a cruder one-shot approximation.

- **Holes vs electrons.** SENSEI's CCDs are "p-channel," meaning the mobile charge carriers are
  *holes* (missing electrons) rather than electrons. The physics is the same; it only changes which
  material constants go into the formulas. The notebook says "carriers" to stay agnostic.

- **Pocket pumping.** The measurement technique. Fill the whole sensor with a roughly uniform sheet
  of charge, then shuffle it back and forth thousands of times. A trap at the right spot repeatedly
  steals charge from one pixel and drops it in the neighbor, building up a visible signature.

- **Dipole.** That signature: two stacked pixels, one darker than average and the one just below it
  brighter by the same amount (charge stolen from one, dropped into the other). The finder hunts for
  these. "Dipole intensity" = how much charge got moved.

- **t_ph (pump dwell / phase time; `dtph` in filenames and stage tables).** The tunable delay of the
  pocket-pumping clock: how long the charge parks on one side of a trap during each pump cycle before
  being shuffled back. Each pumping image is taken at one t_ph; scanning it (~80 µs up to ~1 s, in
  15 MHz sequencer ticks — that tick count is the `dtph` in filenames) traces out the
  intensity-vs-delay curve whose shape measures the trap's emission time τ. The model's emission
  window is `[t_ph, 8·t_ph]` because the opposite park lasts 7× longer (the pump duty ratio).

- **Clock phases / gates (V1, V2, V3).** Each pixel is covered by three electrodes ("gates" or
  "phases"); raising and lowering their voltages in sequence is what moves charge from row to row
  ("clocking"). Which gates hold the charge during exposure, between transfers, and during pumping
  is set by the sequencer recipes (`daq/*.xml`) — and it matters, because a trap sits under one
  specific gate, and that determines how long it sees charge and whether pumping can detect it at
  all. In the current simulation kernel, "V1 trap" vs "V3 trap" distinguishes whether the packet
  crosses the trap on the way *into* or *out of* a row transfer. One polarity subtlety: these are
  **p-channel** CCDs (the carriers are holes), so the charge collects under the most *negative* —
  i.e. the **non-asserted** — gate in a sequencer state; during readout the holes rest under V2 and
  V1/V3 are the barriers (see [physics](physics.qmd) §2.4 for the full gate-role derivation).

- **Dark current.** Charge that accumulates in a pixel over time even with no light, from thermal
  effects. It grows quickly as the sensor warms up, which is why high-temperature images are noisier
  and have the "pedestal" problem below.

- **Single electron / 1e⁻ / SER.** The dark-matter search looks for pixels containing exactly one
  electron. **SER** = "single-electron rate," how many such pixels appear per pixel per image. Traps
  are a worry because a released trapped electron adds a fake 1e⁻ count. The whole project asks: how
  much do traps shift the SER?

- **Pedestal (readout-deferral / CTI pedestal).** A constant, always-present dipole that a trap
  makes *during readout* (not during pumping) by deferring some of the dark-current background as it
  is clocked past. It grows with temperature. It matters because the old fit model had no place to
  put it, so it corrupted the fits at high temperature — the central discovery of the signed-refit
  thread. **CTI** = "charge transfer inefficiency," the general phenomenon of charge getting left
  behind during clocking.

- **V_p (packet volume, `--packet-volume-um3`).** The effective volume (in cubic microns, ~1–10, code
  default 3) that a single electron explores inside a pixel well. The simulation needs it to turn a
  cross-section into a capture *rate* (rate needs a density = charge / volume). It is not directly
  measured, so it is carried as a systematic uncertainty (a knob varied to bracket the answer).

- **Quadrant.** A CCD is read out through four corner amplifiers (UL/UR/LL/LR), dividing it into four
  quadrants. Each has slightly different noise and dark current, so many quantities are tracked
  per-quadrant. Indices 0–3.

## The catalog: two analysis pipelines

- **Legacy pipeline (`dipole.py`).** The original analysis. Simpler, but its fit model breaks above
  ~165 K. Kept as a comparison baseline.

- **Minimal pipeline (`dipole_new.py`).** The corrected analysis used going forward. "Minimal"
  because it is the *smallest* set of physically-required fixes to the legacy method — not a
  ground-up rewrite. Turned on with `--pipeline minimal`. See [dipole_algorithm](dipole_algorithm.qmd).

- **"caldet" / `minimal_caldet`.** Short for "calibrated detection." The minimal pipeline run with
  `--detection calibrated` (the honest, data-measured detection threshold rather than a fixed
  guessed number). The current production catalog file is `fit_dipole_spectra_minimal_caldet_err_4.h5`.

- **Finder.** The first stage: scans images for dipole-shaped pixel pairs and produces a list of
  candidate trap locations. Finding a candidate is *not* the same as confirming a trap.

- **Characterized / well-behaved trap.** A candidate that survived all the quality cuts: it was
  cleanly measured at enough temperatures (≥4) and its τ-vs-temperature points fit the SRH law. Only
  characterized traps enter the catalog and seed the simulation. ("Well-behaved" specifically = the
  ≥4-good-temperatures requirement.)

- **Good temperature / good fit.** A trap counts as measured "well" at one temperature if its
  intensity-vs-delay curve passes the per-temperature cuts there. A trap needs ≥4 good temperatures
  to be characterized.

- **Signed vs absolute intensity.** The legacy method threw away whether a dipole pointed up or down
  (took the absolute value). The minimal method keeps the sign, because a real trap always pumps in
  the same direction — a sign that flips across temperatures reveals contamination.

- **Orientation consistency.** The cut that uses the sign: a single real trap's significant
  temperatures should all share one sign. Mixed signs → flagged as contamination
  (`dual_response`, `ambiguous_sign_conflict`) and rejected.

- **Decoy / decoy control.** A deliberately fake "trap" (a random or wrong-shaped location) run
  through the whole pipeline to measure how often junk sneaks into the catalog. Shows that *detection*
  alone is a weak filter but full *characterization* rejects ~97–99% of decoys.

- **Calibrated detection threshold.** Instead of guessing how strong a signal must be to count as
  real, measure it: run the exact fit on thousands of empty (trap-free) control locations and set the
  bar where only 0.1% of pure noise would pass, separately for each temperature. See
  [dipole_algorithm](dipole_algorithm.qmd) §3.1.

## The simulation

- **MINOS vs SNOLAB.** Two operating scenarios. MINOS (a shallower site) sees more high-energy
  background events; SNOLAB (deep underground) sees ~10× fewer. The simulation runs both.

- **HEE (high-energy event).** A bright track or blob from a cosmic ray or radioactive decay —
  thousands of electrons, far above the single-electron signal. The simulation transplants them
  from a real image. They matter twice over: they drive the masking, and they are the main charge
  source that *fills the traps* (occupancy), which sets the scale of the trap effect.

- **Trap branch vs no-trap branch.** Every simulated exposure is run twice with the *same* injected
  charge — once with traps, once without. Subtracting the two isolates the trap effect and cancels
  the shared randomness ("common random numbers").

- **Exposure-dependent vs exposure-independent (slope vs intercept).** The single-electron rate is
  fit as `rate = intercept + slope × exposure_time`. The **intercept** ("exposure-independent") is
  the part present even in a zero-length exposure; the **slope** ("exposure-dependent") is the part
  that grows with how long the sensor collects. Traps affect both.

- **Masking.** The real experiment discards pixels near bright events and noisy columns before
  counting single electrons. The simulation reproduces this (via `hotcol.py`) so the "masked" trap
  excess is what actually survives into the science result — usually far smaller than the raw excess.

- **Upper-limit population.** Because the measurement misses some faint/hidden traps, the simulation
  is also run with an *inflated* trap population (efficiency-corrected, 90%-confidence). This is a
  "what if the true population were this large" bound, not a measured number. ~17,500 traps vs ~3,800
  characterized.

- **Deviation budget.** A line-by-line accounting of *every* reason the simulated single-electron
  count differs from the injected truth — each with a formula, a sign (does it add or subtract
  electrons?), and how it changes with exposure time. The point is to understand the trap effect as a
  sum of named, physical mechanisms rather than one opaque number. It is [physics](physics.qmd) §4.

- **Instrumented run / kernel.** A special simulation run where every electron is tagged and its fate
  tracked (captured, emitted, re-captured, masked, lost…). Used to *directly measure* the mechanisms
  in the deviation budget instead of only reasoning about them. The "kernel" is the resulting measured
  response.

- **Clear modes (`--clear-mode`).** How the sensor is reset between simulated images:
  `sequencer` (the realistic default), `three_hour` (a long 3-hour drain), `binned_0h` (no clear),
  `instantaneous` (an idealized legacy option). They differ in how much trapped charge survives to the
  next image. Detailed in `CLAUDE.md`.

- **The three recapture models (physics history — know which is current).** How the simulation treats
  a trap capturing charge during readout went through three versions: **Model A** (no recapture —
  made 97% of traps inert, wrong), **Model B** (full-row recapture — too strong, contradicted the
  pumping data), and **Model C = `phase_limited_v1v3`** (capture only in a brief 20-microsecond
  window as charge crosses the trap — **the current, live model**). See [physics](physics.qmd) §2.

## The completeness study

- **Completeness.** "Did we catch the traps that exist?" Specifically, the probability that a trap of
  a given τ135 and energy would have been detected and characterized if it were there. The worry is a
  large *hidden* population of long-lived traps.

- **Survivorship (selection) bias.** The trap that breaks the naive method: if you estimate "how
  complete are we?" using only the traps you already caught, you are blind to the ones you missed by
  construction. The whole point of Method 3 is to escape this.

- **Method 1 / 2 / 3.** Three approaches to completeness. Method 1 (efficiency ratio) is in the
  original paper and is survivorship-biased. Method 2 (band coverage) is a stepping stone. **Method 3**
  (analytic injection-recovery) is the chosen one. See [completeness_efficiency](completeness_efficiency.qmd).

- **Injection-recovery.** Plant fake traps of known properties into realistic simulated data, run the
  real pipeline, and see what fraction come back. The recovered fraction is the detection efficiency —
  measurable *without* reference to the real trap population, which is how it dodges survivorship bias.

- **p_det.** The output of injection-recovery: the probability of detecting a trap of a given
  emission time and brightness at a given temperature.

- **Amplitude prior.** The assumed distribution of trap brightnesses, calibrated from the brightest
  (least-biased) measured traps. It is the one remaining place the real population sneaks into
  Method 3, so it is isolated and stress-tested ("faint-by-2 / faint-by-4" variants).

- **D_t and P_c (the pieces of a dipole's amplitude).** The fitted pump amplitude decomposes as
  `A = N_pumps · D_t · P_c`: **N_pumps** = 3,000 pump cycles per image; **D_t** = the trap "depth,"
  how much charge it moves per cycle when it fires; **P_c** = the probability the trap actually
  captures a carrier in a given cycle. `P_c(T)` falling at high temperature is a *real* warm-T
  incompleteness signal (Stage 05 of the completeness chain).

- **Poisson-binomial.** The bit of math that combines per-temperature detection probabilities into
  "probability of ≥4 successes across 23 temperatures." (A binomial where each trial has a different
  success probability.)

- **WS1 / WS2 / WS3 (work-streams).** Three fixes to the Method-3 implementation. **WS1** = the
  noise-injection bug fix (was injecting the wrong noise level). **WS2** = sharing one identical
  energy-fit function between the live code and the forward model. **WS3** = the check (later retired
  as unnecessary) of whether the energy-fit step erodes completeness; conclusion was that it costs
  only ~4%. See [completeness_efficiency](completeness_efficiency.qmd) §5.

- **POP1 / POP2.** Two populations of high-temperature fit failures found in the residual audit.
  **POP1** = genuinely faded traps (real signal loss — a true incompleteness). **POP2** = real traps
  whose curve shape trips the goodness-of-fit cut but whose τ is fine (recoverable). Distinguishing
  them bounds how much the completeness is over-claimed.

- **The "naive dip."** A dip in the paper's original efficiency curve at high temperature that looked
  alarming. Shown to be mostly an artifact of an over-strict statistical cut, not a real loss of
  sensitivity. See [completeness_efficiency](completeness_efficiency.qmd) §6.

- **survival(k).** A discarded correction factor (keyed on a trap's good-temperature count) that
  created a spurious dip in one completeness curve by mixing up "did we catch it" with "is it
  contamination." Removed from the code.

## Statistics terms

- **Goodness-of-fit (GOF).** A test of whether a fitted curve actually describes the data. Two are
  used: a **p-value** and a **reduced χ²** (see next two).

- **χ² (chi-squared) and reduced χ².** χ² measures total mismatch between a fit and the data (scaled
  by the error bars). **Reduced χ²** divides by the degrees of freedom; ≈1 means "fits as well as the
  noise allows," ≫1 means "the model is wrong or the errors are underestimated."

- **dex.** A factor of ten on a logarithmic scale: "0.1 dex" means a factor of 10^0.1 ≈ 1.26,
  "1 dex" a factor of 10. Used throughout for offsets in log τ (e.g. "the hot points sit
  0.14 dex below the line" = a factor ~1.4 short).

- **Degrees of freedom (dof).** The number of data points minus the number of fitted parameters. A
  subtle but important point in this project: a p-value cut gets *stricter* as you add more data
  points (more dof), which perversely throws away the *best-measured* traps — the reason the project
  switched to a reduced-χ² cut, which doesn't have that problem.

- **p-value.** The probability of seeing data at least this discrepant if the model were correct. A
  common cut is "reject if p < 0.05," but here that cut was shown to be biased (see dof, above).

- **False-positive rate (FPR).** How often pure noise (a trap-free location) passes as a real
  detection. The calibrated catalog targets ~0.1% per temperature and achieves ~0.01% overall.

- **Selection / Malmquist bias.** A bias created by selecting on a noisy measured quantity near a
  boundary. Here: keeping only cold-temperature traps whose noisy τ happens to land inside the
  measurable window biases the surviving τ values short, which tilts the fitted energy. Named after
  the analogous effect in astronomy (brighter objects preferentially detected).

- **Wilks' theorem.** The statistical result that *justifies* treating a certain fit-improvement
  statistic as a standard χ². It requires "regularity" conditions that are violated here (a parameter,
  τ, becomes undefined when the signal is zero), which is why a fixed "3-sigma" threshold was wrong
  and had to be replaced by a directly-measured one.

- **Look-elsewhere effect.** If you scan many possibilities (here, many candidate τ values) and keep
  the best, you get a good-looking result by chance more often than a single test would. Must be
  accounted for when setting thresholds.

- **GLS (generalized least squares) / profile fit.** GLS = a fit that accounts for correlated noise.
  "Profile fit in τ" = instead of fitting all parameters at once (which can get stuck), step through
  a grid of fixed τ values, solve the easy linear part at each, and keep the best — robust against the
  fit landing in a bad local minimum.

- **Overdispersion (φ, phi).** A fudge factor multiplying the expected noise to make it match the
  observed scatter. In the signed-refit thread the data demanded φ = 8–30×, which was a red flag that
  the noise model was wrong rather than a legitimate small correction — a key reason the full
  machinery was rejected.

- **absolute_sigma / errors_are_absolute.** A fitting-library setting. When off (the legacy bug), the
  fit quietly rescales the reported uncertainties by the fit quality, corrupting every downstream
  significance cut. When on, the supplied error bars are trusted as real. The minimal pipeline turns
  it on.
